title: Settlement Optimization Is a Process, Not a Setting
summary: Settlement times can change. Learn how direct payment rails, treasury operations, and regular reviews can help businesses access funds faster. The post Settlement Optimization Is a Process, Not a Setting appeared first on Xendit .
body_markdown:
Compare notes with other businesses and settlement numbers rarely line up. Two businesses accept the same payment method, in the same market, in the same currency. One could be quoted T+2 by their provider, meaning funds reach their account two days after the transaction, the other quoted T+4.


Nothing went wrong. Each was given a number that was accurate on the day it was quoted. Most never look underneath that number, because unless it's drastically different from what they expected, they don't feel a need to.


They should. The gap between T+2 and T+4 is two days of revenue sitting in someone else's account, on every transaction. Most of it comes down to three things a merchant can ask about.


## **There's no universal settlement clock**


Ask a merchant what T+2 means and most will describe it as a property of the payment method. Cards take a few business days, e-wallets are quicker. "That's just how the rails work" comes up in a lot of sales calls, and it's close enough to true that it can go years without being tested.


What it misses is that a settlement time describes a chain of parties. A card payment passes from the issuing bank to the card scheme, then to a bank acquirer, then to the payment provider, then to the merchant. A QRIS or e-wallet payment runs a shorter chain, but it is still a chain. Each node in the chain has its own cutoff times and funding schedule, and any of them can change without the merchant hearing about it. New national payment rails change what's possible too, which is why ASEAN member states have spent years building


[a common policy framework for real-time retail payments](https://asean.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/ASEAN-Policy-Brief-4_FINAL-06Apr2021-1.pdf) rather than assuming settlement times would converge on their own.


Two things keep these changes from surfacing:


- Settlement time gets presented once during onboarding, alongside the fee schedule and integration docs, and nothing in the relationship afterward prompts a second look.


- Merchants only push back when one payment provider is a visible outlier against the others in their stack. When everyone quotes something similar, there's no signal telling anyone that similar isn't the same as current.


There's a practical reason for some of it as well. A payment provider working with several bank acquirers for cards can't always quote a different settlement time for each one without handing merchants a schedule too complicated to plan around, so many default to the slowest one.


## **Three questions that explain the gap**


When two merchants get different settlement times for the same payment method, the difference usually traces back to one of three things.


**1. Is your payment provider connected directly to the rails, or through another provider?**


Many payment providers don't connect to every payment method themselves. To cover a market, they connect to another payment provider that does, and sometimes that provider connects to a third. The merchant sees one provider and one contract. Underneath, there may be two or three.


Each provider in that chain needs time to receive funds, reconcile them and pay them onward, usually at least a business day. Stack two providers and a merchant can lose two days before the money reaches them, on a payment method that funds faster than either. Few providers volunteer whose connections sit underneath their coverage, so it's worth asking directly.


The answer isn't for merchants to contract every bank acquirer and e-wallet themselves. A merchant with one payment provider has one settlement relationship to monitor. A merchant with five direct relationships has five, each drifting on its own schedule, each needing someone in-house to notice when it drifts. What shortens settlement is fewer layers between your provider and the payment rail, not more relationships for you to manage.


**2. How quickly can each provider move the money once it lands?**


Settled doesn't necessarily mean available. When a payment method funds a payment provider, the money lands in a specific account, held by a specific entity, in a specific currency. If it then needs to reach a merchant in another entity, currency or market, someone has to move it. How fast that happens depends on the provider's treasury function: how much liquidity it keeps where, and how quickly it can rebalance.


This matters most for cross-border payments. Domestic settlement is faster because funds rarely need to cross entities or currencies. For cross-border, a payment method funding on T+2 doesn't mean your provider can pay you on T+2. If your provider sits on top of another provider, both treasury functions are in the path.


**3. Does your provider review its terms, and pass the improvement on?**


Settlement terms between payment providers and payment methods don't stand still either. E-wallets improve their funding schedules, bank acquirers renegotiate, national payment rails add faster options. A provider that reviews its contracts regularly will find room to settle faster.


What happens next is where providers differ. Faster funding from a payment method can simply stay with the provider, sitting in its account a little longer and earning interest. Very few providers go back to merchants unprompted to say they can now offer T+2 instead of T+3. Most merchants have never had that call, which is reason enough to ask when their terms were last reviewed.


## **How Xendit answers those three questions**


Xendit is a principal member of Visa and Mastercard and a direct acquirer on national QR payment rails including QRIS and DuitNow, with eight to twelve direct bank connections per market. Fewer hops between the payment rail and the merchant means less time added along the way.


Direct connections only shorten settlement if we can move the funds onward just as fast. That depends on liquidity being positioned in the right entity, in the right currency, before the money arrives rather than after. A provider holding a thin position in a market has to wait for funds to land and clear before it can settle onward, which quietly adds a day back. The improvements we publish are ones our treasury team has confirmed we can fund domestically.


We also review settlement terms on a cycle rather than once at signing. Each review checks how quickly every payment method funds us against the settlement time we offer merchants, market by market. Where a payment method has improved, we update our settlement time to match and pass the benefit along to the merchant.


Our latest review is improving settlement times for


18 payment methods across Southeast Asia, including virtual accounts, national QRs (QRIS) and e-wallets (GoPay, DANA, Maya, ShopeePay and GrabPay), with many now settling at T+1 or even instantly.


Merchants don't need to ask for it. We're passing the improvement on as it rolls out.


## **The review that's easy to skip**


Settlement doesn't need to be the loudest item on anyone's optimization list. It just needs to be on it. The settlement time in your contract was likely the best your provider could offer when you signed. Whether it's still the best they can offer today is a separate question, and it only gets answered if somebody asks.


So ask your payment provider, us included, the three questions above: who sits between you and the payment rail, how quickly they can move money once it lands, and when your terms were last reviewed.
